passages.title: The Second Life of a Shirt
passages.passage:
A. Wardrobes in wealthy countries now shed clothing at a rate that would have astonished earlier generations. A garment bought in the spring, worn a handful of times and dropped into a charity bin by autumn has not, however, reached the end of its life; it has merely entered a second market, with its own prices, middlemen and peculiar logic. Far from being a sideline to the fashion industry, the trade in used clothing has become a global business worth billions, and it rewards close study precisely because so few of the people who feed it ever think about where their donations go.

B. The first surprise is how little of what is donated is sold where it was given. A charity shop on a European high street can display only a fraction of what arrives at its back door; the rest is sold by the kilo to sorting firms, whose graders flick each item into one of dozens of bales according to type, condition and likely destination. A wool coat may be routed to Eastern Europe, a summer dress to West Africa, a pair of jeans with a fashionable label to a vintage dealer in Tokyo. What looks like charity at one end of the chain is, by the middle, a commodity business in which margins are thin and volume is everything.

C. The second surprise concerns who pays. Bales arriving at a port in Ghana or Kenya are bought sight unseen by traders, who gamble that the contents will contain enough saleable pieces to cover the cost. Open a bale and the gamble is revealed: a few prized items, many ordinary ones and a stubborn residue too worn, too stained or too unsuited to the climate to be sold at all. That residue, which by some estimates amounts to a third of every bale, ends up in landfill or in rivers, so that the environmental burden of overproduction is quietly shifted from the countries that bought the clothes new to those that inherit them used.

D. Defenders of the trade point out, not unreasonably, that it employs enormous numbers of people and clothes many more at prices they can afford. Critics reply that the flood of cheap imports has hollowed out local garment industries that once thrived. Both are right, which is what makes the question so hard to settle. Had the imports never arrived, domestic tailors might have prospered; had they been banned, as several governments have attempted, the traders, porters and repairers who now depend on the trade would have lost their livelihoods overnight.

E. What is clearer is that the whole system rests on a fiction: the belief, held by the donor, that giving a garment away absolves them of responsibility for it. Nothing in the economics supports this. The value of a donated shirt is set not by the generosity of the giver but by what a sorter in one country and a trader in another are willing to pay for it, and when the answer is nothing, the shirt does not vanish. Any serious reckoning with the waste of the fashion industry will therefore have to begin at the point where clothes are made and sold, rather than at the bin where their first owners stop thinking about them.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) describes how donated clothing is classified and sent to different countries?
questions.explanation: Section B describes the graders 'flicking each item into one of dozens of bales' and gives the destinations: Eastern Europe, West Africa, Tokyo.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) describes goods being bought before anyone has examined them?
questions.explanation: In section C the bales 'are bought sight unseen by traders, who gamble' on what they contain.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) accepts that two opposing views are both partly correct?
questions.explanation: Section D sets out the defenders' and the critics' cases and then says 'Both are right, which is what makes the question so hard to settle'.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) argues that the waste problem must be tackled at an earlier stage in a garment's life?
questions.explanation: Section E concludes that any reckoning with fashion waste 'will have to begin at the point where clothes are made and sold, rather than at the bin'.

questions.q: What is the writer's main purpose in the passage?
options: To show that the trade in used clothing is a large, complex business whose true costs are hidden from the people who donate
To argue that governments should ban the import of second-hand garments
To explain why vintage clothing has become fashionable in wealthy countries
To persuade readers to stop giving their old clothes to charity shops
questions.explanation: Each section reveals a 'surprise' about the trade (its scale, its routes, who pays) and the last returns to the donor's ignorance of it. The writer never tells readers to stop donating, and treats bans as a two-sided question.

questions.q: Why does the writer point out in section A that few donors think about where their clothes go?
options: To criticise donors for being less generous than earlier generations
To suggest that the trade has escaped scrutiny despite its enormous size
To explain why charity shops receive more clothing than they can sell
To show that the second market is a recent development
questions.explanation: The trade 'rewards close study precisely because' its suppliers never look at it: a billion-dollar business that its own suppliers ignore is one nobody has been examining. Generosity and the shops' capacity are not the point of the sentence.

questions.q: In section D, 'hollowed out' is closest in meaning to
options: modernised
exposed to view
weakened from within
moved elsewhere
questions.explanation: To hollow something out is to remove its substance while leaving the shell; the local industries 'that once thrived' have been emptied of their strength by cheap imports.

questions.q: Traders at African ports are able to inspect the contents of a bale before agreeing a price.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: Section C says the bales are 'bought sight unseen' and that the contents are only revealed once a bale is opened, so the statement contradicts the passage.

passages.title: The Colour That Came Last
passages.topic: why some languages have no word for blue
passages.passage:
Readers of ancient Greek poetry have long been puzzled by its colours. The sea is 'wine-dark', honey is 'green', and the sky is scarcely given a colour at all. [1] The more likely explanation, is that the poets were not seeing differently but naming differently: their language had no word that carved out blue as a category of its own.

They were not unusual. When researchers compared the colour vocabularies of dozens of unrelated languages, a striking pattern emerged. Every language had terms for dark and light. If it had a third term, that term was red. Yellow and green came next, in either order, and blue arrived only after them, if at all. [2] A language with two colour words would never possess 'blue' but lack 'red'; the sequence ran in one direction only.

Why blue should be the straggler has several plausible answers, none complete. One points to the scarcity of blue in the world our ancestors handled: there are few blue foods, blue animals or blue stones, and the blue of sky and sea, being neither an object nor a surface, may not have seemed to need a name. [3] Cultures that acquired the means to produce a stable blue pigment tend, it turns out, to have acquired a word for it at roughly the same time, as though the ability to make a colour is what finally fixes it in the language.

None of this means that speakers of a blue-less language cannot see blue. Their eyes are the same as anyone else's. What differs is how quickly and reliably they sort what they see. In one experiment, speakers of a language that groups blue and green under a single term took measurably longer than English speakers to pick out a blue square from a set of green ones, yet were quicker to spot a subtly different green that English lumps together with its neighbours. [4] The vocabulary does not build the eye, but it does tune the attention.

The lesson runs the other way too. Russian, unlike English, obliges its speakers to choose between two words for what we call blue, one for the lighter shade and one for the darker, and Russian speakers tell those two shades apart faster than English speakers do. [5] Colour, which feels like the least negotiable of our perceptions, turns out to be partly a matter of the words we have been handed; and the sky, which has been blue for as long as there have been eyes to look at it, waited a surprisingly long time for anyone to say so.

A. Another looks not at nature but at manufacture.
B. Children, tellingly, learn the names of colours in much the same order.
C. Some early scholars concluded from this that the Greeks must have suffered from a collective defect of vision, a theory that did not survive long.
D. Having a word, it seems, does not merely record a distinction; it sharpens it.
E. The order was not merely common; it was, as far as anyone could tell, without exception.
F. Greek painters, by contrast, used blue pigments freely, which only deepens the mystery.
G. The distinction their language insists upon, in other words, is precisely the one their perception has been trained to make.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [1]?
questions.explanation: C offers the theory of a 'defect of vision', which is what 'the more likely explanation' in the next sentence is being compared with. F adds a new puzzle rather than a theory, so 'more likely' would have nothing to answer.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [2]?
questions.explanation: E says the order was 'without exception', which the next sentence illustrates ('would never possess blue but lack red'). B raises children, whom the passage never mentions again.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [3]?
questions.explanation: 'One points to…' is followed by 'Another looks…', and 'manufacture' sets up the sentence about cultures that learned to 'produce a stable blue pigment'.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [4]?
questions.explanation: G sums up the experiment ('in other words'): the distinction the language makes is the one perception has been trained on, leading to 'the vocabulary… does tune the attention'.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [5]?
questions.explanation: D draws the conclusion from the Russian example: having a word 'sharpens' a distinction, which is why Russian speakers separate the two blues faster.

questions.q: Which statement best summarises the writer's conclusion?
options: The words a language provides affect how readily its speakers notice colour differences, without changing what their eyes can see
Ancient Greek poets deliberately avoided naming the colour of the sky
Every language eventually develops the same set of colour terms
Languages without a word for blue are spoken by people who cannot see it
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph states that eyes are the same and 'what differs is how quickly and reliably they sort what they see'; the final paragraph calls colour 'partly a matter of the words we have been handed'. The Greeks were not deliberately avoiding anything, and the passage says blue arrives 'if at all'.

questions.q: Why does the writer mention that there are few blue foods, animals or stones?
options: To prove that early humans lived far from the sea
To show that blue is a rarer colour than red in nature
To explain why blue pigments were expensive to produce
To suggest that people tend to name only what they need to handle or use
questions.explanation: The list is followed by the remark that sky and sea, 'being neither an object nor a surface, may not have seemed to need a name': the implication is that a colour is named when it belongs to things people deal with. The passage compares nothing with red's frequency and says nothing about the cost of pigment.

questions.q: In the third paragraph, 'the straggler' refers to
options: the one that appears most frequently
the exception that proves the rule
the one that falls behind the others
the most disputed case
questions.explanation: A straggler is someone who lags behind a group; blue is the colour term that 'arrived only after' the others, so the word describes its late position in the sequence.

passages.title: What Holds a Bridge Up
passages.passage:
A. Ask a child to draw a bridge and you will get a plank laid across a gap. For short spans it is also a correct one: a beam resting on two supports carries a load by bending, its upper surface squeezed and its lower surface stretched. The trouble begins when the gap widens. Double the length of a beam and the bending force at its middle does not double but quadruples, so that a plank which spans a stream will sag hopelessly across a river. Every other bridge form is, in one way or another, an attempt to escape that arithmetic.

B. The arch escapes it by refusing to bend at all. Shape the structure as a curve, and the weight pressing down on its crown is turned into a squeezing force that travels along the arch and into the ground at either end. Stone, which cracks the moment it is stretched but tolerates almost any amount of squeezing, is therefore the ideal arch material, which is why the Romans could build arches that still carry traffic two thousand years later while leaving no stone beam of any length behind them. The price is paid at the ends: the ground must be able to resist the outward thrust, and where it cannot, the arch spreads and falls.

C. The suspension bridge inverts the logic. Instead of pushing the load into the ground, it hangs the roadway from cables draped over tall towers and anchored at either shore, so that the main members are in pure tension. Steel wire, which is extraordinarily strong when pulled, allows such a bridge to leap gaps that no arch could attempt. Yet lightness brings a vulnerability of its own. A deck that weighs little relative to its span can be set swaying by wind, and if the rhythm of the gusts happens to match the natural rhythm of the deck, each push arrives just as the structure is already moving that way, and the motion grows. Engineers learned this watching a newly opened bridge twist itself apart in a wind that a heavier structure would not have noticed.

D. Modern designers therefore spend as much effort taming movement as they do resisting weight. Decks are shaped in wind tunnels so that air flows past them cleanly; heavy pendulums are hung inside towers to swing against any oscillation; and cable-stayed bridges, in which the deck is held by straight cables fanning out from the towers, offer a stiffer alternative for spans too long for a beam and too short to justify a suspension bridge. What has changed is the ability to model, before a single pile is driven, how a structure will respond to every load it is likely to meet.

E. For all that, the forces that eventually bring most bridges down are humbler than wind. Water finds its way into a joint, rusts a bearing, freezes and expands, and does so unremarked for decades, because inspection is unglamorous and budgets favour whatever can be photographed at an opening ceremony. The engineering of bridges, in the end, is not only the art of making a structure stand but the discipline of keeping it standing, and the second of these has always been harder to pay for than the first.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) explains that the difficulty of spanning a gap grows faster than the gap itself?
questions.explanation: Section A says that doubling a beam's length makes the bending force 'not double but quadruple', and calls this 'that arithmetic'.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) explains why a certain material suits one kind of bridge but not another?
questions.explanation: Section B explains that stone 'cracks the moment it is stretched but tolerates almost any amount of squeezing', which makes it ideal for arches but useless for beams.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) describes measures taken to stop a structure moving dangerously?
questions.explanation: Section D lists wind-tunnel shaping, pendulums inside towers and the stiffer cable-stayed design, all aimed at 'taming movement'.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) suggests that bridges are neglected for reasons that have nothing to do with engineering?
questions.explanation: Section E blames unglamorous inspection and budgets that 'favour whatever can be photographed at an opening ceremony'; the obstacle is money and attention, not technical knowledge.

questions.q: What does the writer imply by mentioning the 'opening ceremony' in section E?
options: Most bridges fail shortly after they are opened
Ceremonies are an important way of testing a new bridge
Money is more readily spent on building new bridges than on caring for existing ones
Photographs of a bridge are useful evidence for inspectors
questions.explanation: Budgets 'favour whatever can be photographed' at an opening, in contrast to unglamorous inspection: the point is that visible new construction attracts funding while quiet maintenance does not. Nothing is said about ceremonies as tests or about early failure.

questions.q: In section D, 'taming' is closest in meaning to
options: predicting
encouraging
measuring
bringing under control
questions.explanation: To tame something is to make it manageable; the devices listed (streamlined decks, pendulums, stiffer cables) all exist to restrain movement, not to measure or predict it.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: How each bridge form answers the same basic problem, and what threatens a bridge once it is built
Why suspension bridges are the safest type for long spans
The use of computer modelling in modern construction
The reasons the Romans built better bridges than modern engineers
questions.explanation: Sections A–C present beam, arch and suspension bridges as different escapes from 'that arithmetic', D covers movement, and E turns to decay and maintenance. Modelling and the Romans are details within that argument.

questions.q: Some stone beam bridges built by the Romans are still in use today.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: Section B says the Romans left 'no stone beam of any length behind them'; it is their arches, not beams, that still carry traffic.

passages.title: A Clock That Nobody Set
passages.passage:
Few domestic arguments are as predictable as the one about bedtime. The parent sees a child exhausted in the morning and wide awake at midnight, and concludes that laziness or the phone is to blame. [1] Around the onset of puberty, the internal clock that governs when we feel sleepy shifts later by as much as two hours, so that a fifteen-year-old told to sleep at ten is, biologically speaking, being asked to do what an adult would find difficult at eight.

The mechanism is chemical. Melatonin, the hormone that signals to the body that night has come, is released later in adolescents than in either children or adults, and it lingers later into the morning as well. [2] Set against that shift is a school timetable which, in most countries, begins earlier for secondary pupils than for primary ones, precisely the reverse of what the biology would recommend. The result is a population of young people who are chronically short of sleep on weekdays and who attempt to repay the debt with long lie-ins at the weekend, pushing the clock later still.

The costs are not trivial. Adolescents who regularly sleep for fewer than eight hours show poorer concentration, lower mood and a weaker ability to lay down new memories, an unfortunate profile in a group whose main occupation is learning. [3] What looks like a personality, in other words, may in part be a symptom.

Screens do play a part, but a subtler one than the usual complaint suggests. The light from a phone held close to the face is bright enough to delay melatonin further, and the content, designed to hold attention, offers no natural stopping point. [4] A teenager scrolling at one in the morning is not the cause of the problem so much as its most visible expression: the device fills a wakefulness that was going to be there anyway.

Where schools have tried later start times, the findings have been consistent. Pupils sleep longer, attendance rises, and lateness, accidents and reported low mood all fall. [5] Yet the case is strengthened by the very fact that so modest an adjustment can change thousands of lives at once. The argument at the bedroom door, it turns out, has been aimed at the wrong target; the teenager and the parent are on the same side, and the opponent is a clock that neither of them set.

A. Yet studies that remove the devices altogether find that the delay shrinks but does not disappear.
B. Caffeine, by contrast, has been shown to have a much smaller effect on teenagers than on adults.
C. Nor is this a small effect confined to a few individuals; it has been recorded across cultures and appears in other mammals as well.
D. Both may be part of the story, but neither is the whole of it, and the larger cause is one that no amount of nagging can address.
E. Adults who work night shifts report a similar pattern of weekend recovery, though for entirely different reasons.
F. Objections, predictably, come from those who must reorganise transport, sports fixtures and parents' working days around the new hours.
G. Irritability, risk-taking and a tendency to doze off in the first lesson are routinely put down to adolescence itself when they are, at least partly, effects of too little sleep.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [1]?
questions.explanation: 'Both' in D refers to laziness and the phone, and 'the larger cause' introduces the shift in the internal clock described in the next sentence.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [2]?
questions.explanation: C insists the melatonin effect is real and widespread, so that 'Set against that shift' in the following sentence has a firmly established shift to refer to. E introduces adult night workers, whom the passage never returns to.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [3]?
questions.explanation: G lists behaviours wrongly 'put down to adolescence itself', which is what 'What looks like a personality… may in part be a symptom' then sums up.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [4]?
questions.explanation: A's 'Yet' concedes that removing screens does not remove the delay, which leads directly to the claim that the phone is 'not the cause… so much as its most visible expression'. B's point about caffeine is never developed.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [5]?
questions.explanation: F raises the objections to later start times, and the next sentence answers them with 'Yet the case is strengthened…'.

questions.q: What does the writer suggest with the closing phrase 'a clock that neither of them set'?
options: Alarm clocks are ineffective for adolescents
Parents should allow teenagers to choose their own bedtime
The real cause of the conflict lies outside the control of both parent and child
Teenagers deliberately stay up late to annoy their parents
questions.explanation: The image places the 'opponent' outside both people: a biological timing that neither chose. The passage argues for later school hours, not for letting teenagers decide bedtimes, and says nothing about deliberate defiance.

questions.q: In the third paragraph, 'lay down' new memories means
options: forget
form and store
write out
rest from
questions.explanation: 'Lay down' here is the collocation used for memory formation: the brain records and stores what has been learned. The context, 'a group whose main occupation is learning', confirms it.

questions.q: Schools that start later have recorded improved examination results.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: The final paragraph lists longer sleep, higher attendance and fewer accidents and low moods, but says nothing about examination results either way.
